utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would you please take the card that is offered to you and read allowed the affirmation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, there's a piece of paper that I'd like to produce to you, and it contains your name, date of birth, and place of birth, and can you verify whether those details are accurate? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And, Mr. Usher, I would also ask that that copy be left with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, are those details accurate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And also on that sheet you see four names which are indicated by person A, person B, person C, and person D. When -- when you give your testimony and when if any of those individuals become relevant, can we use the -- the letter rather than the name itself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Because you're a protected witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I seek to tender that document under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As exhibit number 274, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, you're another one of those impressive individuals who can speak more than one language. I believe that B/C/S is your original language, but you'd prefer to speak in English today; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we could just go into private session in relation to some particular details of this individual.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, you were raised in Vukovar; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you lived there with your stepfather and mother?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: At the time that you were raised, were you aware of the ethnic make-up of the town of Vukovar, what main ethnic groups were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: No, sir. I was never -- that was never an issue or topic in my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And in June 1990, did you complete your schooling and were you enrolled for university?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And is it the case that you deferred university and undertook your national service with the JNA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: In what month did you start your national service?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: 17th September, 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And where did you first do your training?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: Slavonska Pozega. I was stationed over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, if I can just ask if you can just take your time a little bit with the answers, especially with names so that they can be fully -- fully recorded.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what was your speciality, your training speciality?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: I was trained over there as a driver, truck driver.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And how long did you train before you were posted somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: Three months, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And where were you posted?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: I was transferred to Kranj, Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And is that on the border between Croatia and Slovenia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: No. That's on the border with Slovenia and Austria.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what was your duty there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: I was a driver, what I was trained for.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what was the duty of the unit there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: We were border unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what was the main role of the unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: Guarding the borders of former Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: If you can just explain to the Court briefly the uniform that the regular JNA soldier had at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: It would be an olive-green colour uniform while I was stationed in Pozega, with the regular black boots, the Tito hat with a star on it, brown belt, typical -- that would be a kind of typical soldier uniform at that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And the Tito hat, would that have any markings on it or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: It had a star on it, yes, red star.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Were helmets ever worn by the regular soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: Yes. But those would be only in situations, let's say, if something would arise, some kind of situation that we have to wear them, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And if the helmets were worn, were there any markings on those helmets?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: There was a red star on it as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Would that be the uniform that the average JNA conscript would wear.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: Yes, sir. That would be a typical soldier uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And as opposed to conscripts that did training, people that were mobilised after they had finished their training, what type of uniform would they wear?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: Mobilised in what sense? Would you mind clarifying that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: If -- if someone had finished their training in the JNA and they were released back to normal duties but were then mobilised, let's say for -- for the war effort, what type of uniform would they wear in relation to the regular conscript that was doing their training or --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: I believe that would be the same uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: In January 1991, did you leave Kranj and go on leave back to Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And before you got to Vukovar, was -- did an incident occur at Vinkovci?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: There was, yes. I'm sorry. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And if you can just explain briefly to the Court what happened to you at Vinkovci before you arrived in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: Well, when we exited the train, it was three of us. The Croatian police at that point -- well, people with the Croatian markings on their -- on their uniforms stopped us and -- which was unusual for that point of -- of time for police, regular civilian police to stop army personnel and ask for their identification. And so they did request it. They stopped us. There were more than three of them. They stopped us. They wanted our identification. They wanted to know where we are, where we are going, what's our ethnicity. They basically harassed us for more than a half an hour, which was really unusual that civilian police would interfere with anything that has to do with the army at that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And after that half an hour did you travel on to Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: They let us go and we went back home. Well, I went home.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And when you say you went home, did you go home to where your family was living in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: Yes. That's where they resided, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And that night did something further occur, and if it did, can you explain what happened to the Court?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: Yes, sir. We went -- we had talked and, you know, I talked to my parents and, you know, we went to bed and around -- I'm not exactly time -- timing but around 1.00, 2.00 in the morning, about four people barged into our apartment, broke to the door, took me out of the bed, pushed my mother on the floor, and took me out, put me in a car. They screamed at me that I'm a Chetnik. Then at that point I was beating -- I was beat up. They were hitting me in the car, you know. They all weared masks. I couldn't see anything there. They were pretty much in civilian clothes at that point. They took me to a forest close, nearby Vukovar. They beat me even more over there, screaming at me like -- that I'm a Chetnik, you know. I'm a soldier, all that kind of stuff. And, you know, they took out a piece of paper where it was typed that, you know, my -- that sentence that they're going to kill me. That's what -- that's what they told me. So they told me to read it out loud, and I was -- since I was really badly beaten at that point, I hardly read the whole sentence, the whole thing that was on the paper. I thought at that point I was going to be killed or -- I didn't know what was going to happen basically, and they made me put that paper in my mouth and swallow it, and they left me over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, I just ask that we -- sometimes I speak a little quickly in the courtroom as well as sometimes your answers are a little quick, so if we can just slow the pace down a bit so that we can record everything that you're saying. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: They left you there. And then how did you -- how did you get back from that location to --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: My mother --

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: -- place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: My mother contacted the police, and I think the military police as well, and they found me in the morning. They brought me to hospital. I ended up with a lot of bruises and stuff. And then after that I was shipped back to my unit, which I never returned to basically. I ended up in the hospital, and I -- I basically used that opportunity to leave the army. I was complaining about psychological trauma that I've been through and, you know, I had a lot of bruises and all this. I didn't wanted to go back anymore to the army. In the situation in our barracks where I served the army was already difficult. They wouldn't let us use the phones to call our families. The situation in Slovenia was difficult at that point. There were -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. If I can just stop you there.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You said that these men called you a Chetnik. What did you think Chetnik meant?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: Well, I guess they referred to me as I'm a Serbian or that I have anything to do with the Serbia or -- I guess Chetnik would be all Serbian army from before the Second World War.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you said that before you got to Vukovar that the Croatian police were harassing you. Can you tell the Court about that time in January 1991, whether there was any tension in and around Vukovar between Croats and Serbs generally?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: Not that I know of, but -- no, I can only speculate about that. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And about how long were you in hospital for?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: About a week and a half to two weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And then you went back to your unit and -- but how long did you stay with your unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: I was released from the hospital and went straight home.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you were released from your military service?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And in 1991, did you go to Belgrade at some point?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: Yes. I went to Belgrade with my sister and my mother in July.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: So from January to -- to July you were living in Vukovar; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And during that time were you aware of any ethnic tensions between the Croats and the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: There were a lot of them, especially close where I used to live.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And can you describe that tension and how it -- how could you see it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: Well, what I could see where I used to live, there was a lot of Croatian army -- there was a lot of -- a huge gathering of Croatian army, people in different military uniforms, wearing the Croatian symbols on their uniforms. They were coming in the cars with no licence plates on. They would call our -- well, I don't know was -- was it them, but, you know, we received a lot of threatening phone calls at home telling that my mom is a Chetnik and we should leave home. There was a lot of -- a lot of threatening phone calls at that point plus very noticeable a lot of police and army of Croatian -- I believe Croatian nationality at that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what -- what part of the town or what area of the town were you living -- living in, just generally?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: I lived very close by to the hospital, to Vukovar general hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And when you stated that you saw a gathering of Croatian army people in different uniforms, was that in the area that you lived, or was it in other areas as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: Right at the location where I used to live, yes. There used to be -- it's -- it used to be a headquarters for a Vupik company, very close to castle of Count Eltz over there, that whole area, and plus Territorial Defence building across the street. It was all full with the Croatian soldiers and police.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did you know if anything else was happening militarily on the other side of the Vuka River, on the south side of the Vuka River --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: -- during that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: No, sir, not at that point. We heard stories, but I didn't see or witness any of -- any of that kind of stuff.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And during that time, between January and July, what -- what were you doing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: Nothing. Basically you couldn't go anywhere. It was unsafe to walk. If it starts getting darker at nights, you would not go outside anywhere. You were basically scared for your life. You heard a lot of different scary stories that were happening around town, and, you know, it was not really -- it wasn't safe for you to go anywhere basically, only during the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And just briefly, why wasn't it safe for you to go anywhere? Are you talking about you in particular or people generally?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: I'm talking people generally at night, or as soon as it starts getting dark, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what was the danger that you felt was there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: There was army all over the place. There was police all over the place. There were these people who were coming, as I said, in -- in those unmarked vehicles, waving their guns, you know, talking about different things that they do at night and, you know -- you know. It wasn't really safe. We felt unsafe, plus all this -- all this harassing phone calls that we were getting at home. I -- we were not really feeling safe to go anywhere at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And so you testified that you went to Belgrade in July; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And can you explain why you went to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: Well, the situation deteriorated a lot. Like it really became very dangerous. You can hear some shooting at night, especially after the 2nd of May when that attack on Borovo Selo happened. You could hear Croatian soldiers singing some national songs about the killings of Serbs, and -- they were all close by to us, and we didn't feel safe anymore. My mom was called so many times. My stepdad was called so many times to leave Vukovar because he lives with a Chetnik. They barged one day into our house, and they took all the weapons that he had. He used to be a hunter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And when you say they barged into your house, who do you mean by "they"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: Croatian police at that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And so where did you stay in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: I stayed with my aunt. At my aunt's house, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And how long did you stay in Belgrade for?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: Almost until mid-October.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what were you doing in those months in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: Well, pretty much I would say I would pretty much be hiding over there. We heard a lot of rumours and seen a lot of -- a lot of mobilisation happening at that point in Belgrade. People were -- people were picked up on the street and taken to -- well, being basically mobilised at that point. You know, I was just scared. I didn't want to go anywhere. We knew that war was going on back -- back at home where we used to live, so -- and we -- I mean, it was noticeable outside that there was a lot of army, a lot of army movement, a lot of military police, and so basically we didn't do much. We pretty much stayed all the time in the house, or if you would go, you would just go to the store and come back.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And where did you go after Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: We went to Bijeljina. We went to Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And why did you go to Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: We felt safer -- safer over there because nothing was happening. There was no war or anything, and plus my mother applied as a refugee and got a place in that -- we got a house to stay in in Bijeljina, so we decided to move. It was much safer for us to go there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And is it the case that you didn't want to be mobilised into the JNA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: That's correct, sir. Not me nor my stepfather.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we could just briefly go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: How long did you stay in Bijeljina for?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: Not into long. Since mid-October until the 4th of November. So about, I would say, 15, 20 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what did you do on the 4th of November?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: I went with a friend of mine that I met in Bijeljina. I went to Sid. Well, we decided to go in Sid. I heard that one of my friends lived in Sid at that point, so I wanted to go and see somebody that I used to live with before. So we decided to take a train and go to Sid.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to ask you a couple of questions about what happened in Sid, and if you could look at the sheet in front of you, and if one of those person's names becomes relevant, if you can just use the letter.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court what happened when you got to Sid?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: When we got to Sid, I noticed there was a lot of -- lot of army, like, I mean, a lot of people dressed in uniforms over there. It was all over the place. And I -- I don't think I've seen any civilian people -- well, at least men in civilian clothes. I noticed one of the -- one of my friends which I'm going to name as the person A on the list who recognised me and asked me to go if I -- well, he said, "Hi, how's everything going," and, you know, kind of started this conversation. And he said, "Well, you know, like let's go somewhere to sit for the coffee," and so we decided well, let's go, let's do it. So on the way to the coffee-shop he said he wants to go and grab some stuff from the house, we were just passing by, so, you know, he said, like, you know, "Well, come in with us," and there were two of them. We got in and they pushed me inside the door basically, me and the other friend of mine, and then I noticed that there was some kind of a military command office at that point. They became very aggressive towards us. They told me to stand over there, which I did at that point. And I was over there, maybe, I don't know, for 15, 20 minutes, maybe a little longer than that. I can't really give exact time, but he left. There were a couple of other soldiers came in, and they -- they through me on the back of the truck, a military truck. They checked our IDs before that; I'm sorry, I forgot to say that. They released my friend because he was from Bosnia. They put me on a military truck together with another three or four people sitting in the truck, in the back, and -- with two guards on the truck as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: If I can -- thank you for that. If I may stop you there. You said at this military command other soldiers came in. Do you know which army they were from or which unit or what type of military grouping they belonged to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: I could not say that, but they were wearing a typical military uniform, typical JNA uniform. I would not -- I can just, you know, estimate at this point. I'm not really sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And at this military command place, this was a house; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And were you being asked questions in this house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: Not -- except taking my -- notes of my ID, couple of details who I am and where I'm from, but not too many questions, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And did they tell you what was -- what was going to happen to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: No, sir. I was not told anything. I was just told to climb on the truck.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And the two guards that you referred to on the truck, what were they wearing and do you know what military grouping they may have belonged to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: They were wearing military uniforms, but they were not really kind of clean looking, I would say. As far as I remember, they had beards. I would say they would be kind of reservists type of personnel at that point. But that's my estimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And reservists of which army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: Of the JNA army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: The military uniforms, what -- what colour were they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: They were all green. They had green long overcoats with the brown belts and black boots, so that would associate me to a typical military uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You may have mentioned this already, but the other four people that were on the truck, did you hear any background information about who they were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: At first when we were -- when I was put on the truck they told us not -- to be silent -- well, to be silent and not to say anything, not to speak at all unless they ask you something. I was so scared at that point I didn't know what to do. I really -- I was in civilian clothes at that point. I thought, like, you know, well, I'm just getting mobilised or something. I don't know what's going on. And no, I was not able to find out anything at that point. Later on when we started moving with the truck and when we, I guess, entered the region where the war was happening, war region I would say, and we stopped a couple times. I guess that would be kind of at check-points or -- those guards would be -- would step from the truck. They would still stay with the truck but they would step off. So at that point I managed to talk to one of them, and he said that he was released from Mitrovica prison, and he was over there for some kind of rape or something. I guess he was a prisoner over there. That's my understanding of what he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what about the other three? Did you find any background information on who they were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: My -- my opinion, I think that they were all -- they all came from the same place. They were not really talking people, but I spoke to one of them. One of them said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And if you can just slow it down one -- one level more, then that would be good for the transcript because we're just missing a couple of words every now and again.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: Yes, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And I think I should slow my question down too because I've missed a couple of words myself. You said that you thought you were being mobilised. Being mobilised into which army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: Into the JNA army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Now, whilst you were in Belgrade and whilst you were in Bijeljina, were you watching the media, the television, reading the papers, as to what was happening in Vukovar before you -- before you went to Sid?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I was -- the war was -- well, media was showing the war and what was all the -- all the happenings there happening around -- around the town of Vukovar and in the close -- close proximity, villages that were around Vukovar. They were showing the war pictures and some footage over there too.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And who was the war between?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: It's my understanding from TV would be that the JNA was trying to liberate Vukovar as a town from Croatian paramilitary organisation or army at that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you said that you were placed on a truck and then you were taken through check-points. Where did you end up?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: I ended up on -- I'm sorry. Am I going too fast?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I think your pace is good now.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: Okay. I -- that night it was dark when we arrived. I ended up in Velepromet. There was -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Had you ever been to Velepromet before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: I've seen that place before, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what was Velepromet used before for?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: That place was used as warehouse, as far as to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Have you ever been in Velepromet before you arrived there that evening?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: I think I've -- I've been couple of times, I think, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And when you got to Velepromet, can you tell the Court what happened initially?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: I was taken off the -- well, all four of us were taken off the truck. Those three guys were taken away or they just, I guess, joined their -- joined their -- a group, wherever they took them. They told me to sit down and wait here. They took my ID from me. And I was sitting and waiting for something to happen. There were a couple of guards at the door, but I was waiting there basically for almost, I don't know, let's say for a longer time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And who took your ID from you? Was it the guards on the truck or was it someone from Velepromet?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: It was -- it was the guards at the Velepromet.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And those guards, do you know what -- what grouping they belonged to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: At that point I didn't know who they belonged to, at that point. Later on I learned that there was -- they were all the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And Territorial Defence of which -- of which army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: Of Vukovar army, I guess. Well, I don't understand the question. Which army?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You're right. It was -- it was a bad question. Do you know the ethnicity of this Territorial Defence that you're referring to --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: I would say --

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: -- of the people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: Serbian I would say, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what happened after that, after your ID was taken from you and you were waiting for something to happen? What happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: One of the people arrived -- well, one of guards came to me and said, you know, is this -- "Is this your name?" And I said yes. And he said, "What are you doing here?" And I said, "Well, I'm not really sure what I'm doing here." At that point I was really -- I was really, really scared. And he said, "Oh, we know what you're doing here." And then he, "Follow me," and he took me to the room where I saw Zigic. He was, I guess, a commander at that point, or whoever, somebody -- somebody in charge in that room.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Can you describe what Zigic was wearing and what he looked like?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: He was wearing a JNA uniform. He was an older person to me at that point. I would say about 40 years old, 45-year-old person. Kind of greyish hair. That's as much as I recall right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And did he ask you any questions in that room? And perhaps when you answer the question, if there's anything in relation to your name if you can just not state your name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Well, he asked me -- he asked me where my father was, my stepfather actually, where I was for all this time, where is my mother, what am I doing here, how did I end up here, you know. He asked me what was I doing downtown Vukovar, because apparently somebody saw me a couple days before on a motorcycle downtown Vukovar while all this fight was happening. And I had no answers for that. I said I was a refugee in Belgrade. I tried to kind of save myself. At that point I was that scared. And when I -- whenever I would not have an answer for him, there was a person that was inside -- in the room with the room with us and he would hit me in the head, sometimes very, very hard. Sometimes he would just slap me in the back. Couple times hit me really, really bad in the head so I fell on the floor. And just repeating all the same questions which I had no answers for. And then, you know, he would smack me with his foot in my stomach and put me back in the chair and asking me again the same questions, you know, where is my stepfather, do I know that he did some bad stuff during whatever, beginning of the war. And I said what -- like that's not possible because he was with us all this time as a refugee, so -- but I asked -- I told him that my mom is Serb. I tried to defend myself as much as I could. But at that point there was no -- there was no -- he wasn't really interested in or understanding any of the answers that I was giving him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. If we can just try to slow it down a fraction.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: This person that was hitting you, do you know who he was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: At that point I didn't know who that was, I mean, but later on when I came back to Velepromet a couple days later, or a couple weeks later, I learned that it was Miroljub Vujovic's body-guard.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Can you say his surname again, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: One -- whose name?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Miroljub's surname.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry. Miroljub Vujovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And after this beating, what happened to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: I was taken to -- I can't call it a prison cell, but I was taken to the room by two guards. It was on the other side of the -- of the Velepromet complex. They put me in a room with about -- about 30 people. From my understanding at that point, it was -- it was a dark room, but I would say about 30 people, all very, very old, as far as I could hear voices of people inside the room. They told me -- they closed the door and locked the door with a chain. I wasn't beat at that point anymore that night, but I found some spot to lie down. It was all concrete. There was nothing on the floor for nobody to sleep on. I could hear through the window that I'm lucky, that -- that some kind of Kosovo guy is not present at Velepromet right now. If he is, you know, he would slaughter me like -- like a chicken very fast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, as far as I know, we continue in morning tomorrow. I'm looking at the transcript and tomorrow morning the transcript might prove useless with so many blanks to be filled. Therefore, what I would like to ask, once again, is to please slow down everyone for the benefit of the transcript, because there are so many blanks in it that I really have no idea how we can have it ready for tomorrow morning. If we had more time to have these blanks filled, that would be fine, but we don't. There are a lot of blanks and what I would like to ask is for the OTP to please try to conduct proceedings at a much slower pace.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I agree with that. I think the witness -- it's a unusual experience and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We appreciate that. If you could just interrupt if the flow is going too fast Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm sure the witness understand, as we understand that he normally speaks fast and the circumstances enhance that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: So, Witness, we'll try and go as slow as we can because your information is important and it's important that it's completely recorded on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: The two guards that took you to this room where you slept, what were they wearing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: I -- I can't remember right now. No, I could not remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: In the room where you slept, were there windows?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: There were window frames, but there were no windows because everything was broken, I guess, because of a war happening around.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And I think you said there were about 30 people in this room.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Were they male or female, and what were the ages of this -- these people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: They would be mostly female as I -- as I recall from the day after when it was daylight and that I could see who was inside in the room with me. Not a lot of male but -- each group would be about around 60 to 70, 65.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Were there any mattresses in the room?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: No, sir. It was bear concrete.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: What was the weather like at that time? What was the temperature like?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: It was very, very cold. I can -- I can say -- there was no -- there was no rain or snow but it was very, very cold.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And in relation to hygiene facilities, like toilets during the night, did you have access to a toilet?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: No, sir. We did not have an access to a toilet. We had a garbage can in the middle of the room which we all used at the same time. Well, for whoever wanted to use it. But basically, yeah, we all used the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: The next morning, what happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: They -- they let us go outside. There was adjacent room to the room where we were held at that point, and you could walk over there for a while. I mean, or you could see what's happening inside a yard or courtyard of a -- of the Velepromet building warehouse, sorry, but nothing -- nothing more at that point. The guards were still standing over there. Some people were going about their duties. I think they were chopping wood, cleaning around.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, just for the record, some of the -- what appear to be blanks nothing is in fact being said by the witness so it may be a little bit misleading as well that something is being missed on the transcript, but that's -- that's not the case on a number of cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, did you see Zigic again that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: Yes, I was taken to his office again later that day, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And did you -- did he speak to you about anything, and if he did, what was it about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: Again, I had the same questions asked, what I was doing over there, what was I doing downtown Vukovar couple -- a couple days ago on the motorcycle, where is my stepfather, how did I end up being here. And then he said, "Now take him away because I haven't decided what to do with him."

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And sometime that day, the first day that you had at Velepromet, did you see someone -- someone you knew?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: Yes, I -- I've seen an acquaintance of mine from school, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And did you say anything to that acquaintance?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: I tried to get his attention, and I tried to speak to somebody like -- because kind of -- I knew that person so I was trying to do whatever to get his attention and so he notices that I'm over there, but he wasn't really interested in coming and talking to me at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And that day did you also see a family friend?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: Yes. I've seen a person be in the courtyard of Velepromet, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did you finally get to speak to your acquaintance and ask him to do something?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: Yes, I did, sir. I managed to ask him if he can go and talk to the person B because I -- he was a family friend and I -- I was trying just to get -- get out of from there. You know, I tried to save my life as fast as I can. So, yes, he did. And he -- he spoke to him, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And did you again stay at Velepromet that night for a second night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I stayed one more night over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And which room did you stay in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: We stayed in the same room that I was brought into the first night.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And were the same conditions there, no mattresses, cold, cramped?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: Same conditions, sir. Nothing changed. It stayed the same every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: What happened on the second day after the second night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: The person B came finally and spoke to me. The first day that I managed to contact him through that acquaintance of mine he didn't come and speak to me that time, but next day he came back, and he said he's going to help me and get me out from there. He went to speak to Zigic. They had some kind of argument because apparently I was not supposed to be released. And then after a while he came back and he said, "Don't worry about anything. I'll take you with me, and I'll be responsible for you." And at that point, a little bit later in the afternoon I was released from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And this person B, was he related to any military grouping? Was he in any military group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: Yes, sir. He was in Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And where did he take you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: He took me to his house close to a place called Petrova Gora. That's -- that's where we stayed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And before I ask you some questions about your stay at this house, in relation to the other 30 people that were in the room with you at Velepromet, were they free to stay or go? Were they free to leave Velepromet?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: No, I don't -- I believe not, sir. They were -- we were all kept during the night under the chain and the door was locked all the time. So I -- I would presume that they were over there as prisoners as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And were you able to find out what any of the ethnicities of these people were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: No, sir, no. I did not, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And for the two days you were at Velepromet, did you see what it was being used as apart from the group that was being locked up there and yourself? What else was happening at Velepromet?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: There was a gas station in the middle of the Velepromet. I could see it clearly from the room that we were kind of -- I would call it an exercise room. The trucks would come in and they would refuel. There was a kitchen over there, I guess a part of a public kitchen. Some soldiers would come and have meals over there. Basically coming in and out of military equipment. Mostly trucks refuelling, like a refuelling station. Taking of -- some trucks left with food supplies. Pretty much the trucks that I've seen there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And military trucks of -- were they military trucks of the JNA or some other military group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: I believe so, the JNA. I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And the types of uniforms that you saw people were wearing in Velepromet, can you explain the types that were being worn?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: There were all kinds of -- all kinds of uniforms. People were wearing some -- some of them would wear the full uniform of -- green uniform as a JNA uniform. Some people would have just bits and pieces of JNA uniform together with some different colour overcoats or different hat styles. Basically there were all kinds of uniforms coming in and out. Some of them were camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you said that trucks came in to refuel. You said some of them were military trucks, JNA military trucks. About how often were they coming in to Velepromet to refuel over the two days that you were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: I don't think I can -- I don't know. Maybe I've seen, like, 10, 15 of them. I don't know what the time-frame would be for them to come in and out.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd ask that Exhibit 262 be placed on the screen, please. If that can be enlarged one more level, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, looking at this photograph on the screen, do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: Yes, sir. That would be Velepromet warehouse.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You mentioned that you were questioned when you first arrived at Velepromet in the evening by Zigic. Can you mark on that photograph with the letter A the room that you were questioned in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: Yes, sir. With the letter A?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: A. Large A. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Can you mark with the letter B the room that you slept in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise. Thank you. I reacted a little bit earlier. We didn't have it on our screens. We have the letter B on the screens. We can see that. But we don't know where the letter A is. Well, now we see letter A as well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, also you mentioned an exercise room which you were taken to during the day. Can you mark that with the letter C, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: Okay. That would be -- this would be kind of a divider wall beside, and then the room would be right here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, what work were these 30 people -- what were they undertaking whilst at Velepromet?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: What I observed when I was over there for those few days, they were mostly doing kind of -- they were cleaning the yard. They were chopping wood. Basically some -- some of those -- some of those physical activities as far as -- as far as I know, what I observed, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Do you know where they were chopping wood on that photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: Where they were chopping wood? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: Would you like me to mark it?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: If you could mark it with a D, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: So they were chopping wood inside that building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: Yeah. There's actually three rooms. There would be kind of a divider here for the third room. That's where the washroom was as well if -- during the day that we were allowed to use.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you've divided the building into the rooms by the red lines; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You also mentioned that military trucks would come in and refuel. Do you know the approximate location where they would do that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: Yes, sir. It was right here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And if you can mark that circle with an E, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: E.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I seek to tender that photograph, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be Exhibit number 275.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, you mentioned earlier that person B, who was an acquaintance of yours, was able to convince Zigic to release you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: The acquaintance actually talked to person B, and then he convinced Zigic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And person B was a friend of your family's; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we could go into private session, please, for a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, we'll refer to this person as person B now. He took you back to a house; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: That's correct. That house that they used during the war, where they lived during the -- all the actions that were happening there, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And how far away was that from Velepromet?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: It's about, I would say, ten minutes walk from Velepromet.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And the house, was that in a Serb or Croat area of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: I would say a mostly Serb area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And when you got to that house and the neighbourhood in which it was in, can you explain whether or not buildings were damaged or undamaged?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: They were not -- they were not visible damage at that point that I could -- that I can recall of, at that specific area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what was the arrangement that you had with person B?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: That he's going --

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: He took you from Velepromet. Was there any understanding between you as far as what you were to do from this point forward?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: My understanding was that he's -- he's going to be responsible for me, and I'm going to stay in his house, and he's going to take me safely to my mother. That's exactly his words.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And when you got to his house, was his family living there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: Yes, sir, his wife and two sons.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And without stating their names, were also another three people staying there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And those -- those three people, were they males?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: At that point, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And did they have any role in the conflict that was occurring in Vukovar, those three males that were staying at the house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: As far as I understood, yes, they were -- they were soldiers at that point, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And were they in the same Territorial Defence unit as person B or do you -- did you not know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: Not at that point I didn't know, but -- no, I didn't know that at that point, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what was the reaction to you staying at the house? How did the family or these other people? What did they think about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: It was a kind of mixed reaction. I wasn't really trusted at that point when I came in, I guess because of my background. But they were okay. I mean, nobody was really rude or anything to me, but kind of you felt tension. At least I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And did you stay at that house until the fall of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: Yes, sir. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And when did Vukovar -- what date did Vukovar fall, from your memory?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: I would describe that as the 18th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And between the time you arrived at the house until the 18th of November, what were you doing for that period?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: I was pretty much stationed in the house. I would go out maybe two or three times a day to the public kitchen to have a meal together with other people or other civilians that were in the area. Taking care of his kids at that point, and staying in the house pretty much. Not going anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And person B and the other three men, what were they doing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: They would leave usually around 6.00 in the morning to 7.00 and go off to their duties.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: And do you know particularly what they were doing during that, say, 11-day period.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: No, sir. I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Were you ever mobilised to join the Territorial Defence whilst you were staying at that house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: Yes, the very next day, sir. I was told -- I was approached by a person called Zarko Amidzic, and he said that I have to be dressed up in the uniform, if I'm planning to stay there, and I have to have a weapon, which person B strongly objected, wouldn't allow me to have anything at that point. I don't know whether it's because of mistrust or whatever it is, but he wouldn't let me have any. After that, two other soldiers came in, and they made me go there to the command house at Petrova Gora and told me I have to put a uniform on and I have to get a weapon, which I did at that point, and I signed up with the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And the name of the person that approached you, what was his surname again?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: Amidzic, yeah. That's spelled correct, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And the two soldiers that made you go to the command house, what were they wearing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: They were wearing JNA uniforms, but they were local people so I would say they were Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And the uniform you were given, what type uniform was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: It was a green old JNA uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you said when Zarko approached you that I think you said that person -- person B objected to -- objected to you being mobilised; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And why did he do that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: He didn't want me to have any weapons. He said, you know, "You're not here for that." You know, "I have full responsibility of you and you're not going to go anywhere. You're going to stay in this house and you're going to be alive, and I'll take you to your mother."

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you ultimately were given a weapon at the Territorial Defence command; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: Yes, sir. When I was dressed up, I got a weapon too. It was an M-48 weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did you keep that weapon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: No. (redacted) -- he took it right away from me, and he said he's going to use it for hunting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just ask that line 37 -- sorry,

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. If you can indicate when it is convenient, Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: It's convenient now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will break now for 20 minutes. If the redaction can be held, we'll break for 20 minutes. Otherwise, we have to break for half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: The redaction can be -- I think it can be held.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We'll resume at 25 past.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, before the break you said that you were ordered to take a uniform and a weapon from the Territorial Defence command centre, and that person B decided to take that weapon away from you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you also said for that, say, 11-day period that you were at person B's house that you would basically stay around the house other than going to this public kitchen, say, two or three times a day; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: We just went for meals, but basically we stayed -- I stayed most of the time in the house, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And about how far was this public kitchen, say, from the house that you were staying at and who was running it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: I think it was run by Territorial Defence or -- I think the Territorial Defence, and it's about three minutes walk from the house where we used to stay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And were only Territorial Defence using the public kitchen or was there any other military groups using it as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: Well, I've seen a lot of people come in over there. I cannot say which military groups used it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And during that 11-day period, were you wearing a uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: Yes. Inside the house, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And also when you went to the public kitchen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: Yes. You had to.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And can you tell the Court how you were feeling at this stage in terms of your safety and what you were doing at that house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: Well, I was feeling more relieved because I had somebody to look after me at that point. It wasn't really -- I wasn't feeling safe going over there because people would sometimes point out at me and said, "Oh, I know who that is," or in that kind of sense, you know. So safety wasn't really -- I don't know. I wasn't feeling safe going over there by myself. I was always going with somebody. But in the house or around the house, I was feeling okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And if you can just explain it briefly, why weren't you feeling safe as opposed to perhaps maybe other people that were in the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: I would say before -- because of my background and that people knew who I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And when you say your background, are you talking about your ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: Yes. My ethnicity, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And then you said that Vukovar fell on the 18th of November. The night -- the night before that, was a woman brought to the house that you were living in by someone there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, sir. One older woman, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And can you explain to the Court what she was saying about her experience in Vukovar, just briefly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: Well, she said that -- I mean, during her time in Vukovar during the war, basically she said that her husband died by trying to get water from the well. He died from shelling. She survived, but she buried the body. And the most surprising thing for us at that point was that she was able to go downtown Vukovar just a couple days before it fell and buy some groceries in Nama, which was a kind of convenience superstore that we had in down, which was really unimaginable for us to understand, how was that possible, but she said she did, so is it true or not, I don't know, but she said that in her story.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And why did you find it unimaginable that she could go to the Nama department store?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: Because of all the shelling. The shelling was just constant. It was falling all over the place. You could hear it. I mean, like during the day as soon as -- starting from early morning until the night. It was just going on and on. You know, I don't see how anybody would feel safe just to walk on the street and go buy -- get some groceries or anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And this woman, do you know whether she was a Serb or a Croat or what ethnic background she had?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: I'm not sure of her ethnicity, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: If I can ask that Exhibit 156 be placed on the screen, please. Thank you. And if we can enlarge the centre of town, the main -- that area there. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, looking at this map on your screen, do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-009
utterances.text: Yes, I do, sir. That's a map of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd ask that we go into private session now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 16th day of March, 2006, at 9.00 a.m. 20 21 22 23 24 25
